---
title: "Variant identifiers"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(biobouncer)
```

One variant can be written in several ways, and a check proves something
different for each of them. This article builds the common forms from VCF
columns, then checks them against the shape of the id, the reference
sequence, the databases that assign record ids, and gnomAD.

The running example is `rs7412`, a C to T change in the APOE gene on
chromosome 19.

## One variant, five written forms

| Form | `source_db` | Identifier | Genome build |
|---|---|---|---|
| gnomAD-style coordinate | `gnomad` | `19-44908822-C-T` | not stated |
| SPDI | `spdi` | `NC_000019.10:44908821:C:T` | GRCh38, through the sequence version |
| HGVS | `hgvs` | `NC_000019.10:g.44908822C>T` | GRCh38, through the sequence version |
| dbSNP | `dbsnp` | `rs7412` | none, a record id |
| ClinVar | `clinvar` | `VCV000017848` | none, a record id |

The first three describe the change itself, and you can build them from a VCF
row. The last two are record ids that a database assigned. The only way to
check them is a lookup.

## Checks at a glance

| Check | Tool | Network |
|---|---|---|
| The id is well formed | any variant source, `pattern` mode | no |
| The change fits the reference sequence | `hgvs` source, `remote` mode | yes |
| The rsID is in dbSNP and not merged into another | `dbsnp` source, `remote` mode | yes |
| The accession exists in ClinVar | `clinvar` source, `remote` mode | yes |
| gnomAD has observed the variant | `gnomad_frequencies()` from bioclients | yes |

Each check is covered below, in this order.

## Build the coordinate forms from VCF columns

A VCF row gives a chromosome, a 1-based position, a reference allele, and an
alternate allele. For a single-base substitution, each coordinate form is a
paste of those four fields.

```{r}
vcf <- data.frame(
  chrom = c("19", "19"),
  pos = c(44908822L, 44908684L),
  ref = c("C", "T"),
  alt = c("T", "C")
)

# The RefSeq accession of each chromosome, in the build the VCF was called on.
# NC_000019.10 is chromosome 19 in GRCh38.
refseq <- c("19" = "NC_000019.10")
acc <- unname(refseq[as.character(vcf$chrom)])
stopifnot(!anyNA(acc))

pos <- as.integer(vcf$pos)

gnomad_id <- paste(vcf$chrom, pos, vcf$ref, vcf$alt, sep = "-")
spdi_id <- paste(acc, pos - 1L, vcf$ref, vcf$alt, sep = ":")
hgvs_id <- paste0(acc, ":g.", pos, vcf$ref, ">", vcf$alt)

data.frame(gnomad_id, spdi_id, hgvs_id)
```

The build has three guards. `as.character()` makes the accession lookup go
by name when the chromosome column is a factor, and `stopifnot()` stops on a
chromosome that has no accession. `as.integer()` keeps the position whole: R
writes a round number stored as a double, such as 20000000, as `2e+07`.

Two details differ between the forms. SPDI counts positions from 0, so its
position is the VCF position minus one. SPDI and HGVS also name a versioned
reference sequence, which fixes the genome build, while the gnomAD-style id
names only the chromosome.

The HGVS paste is correct for single-base substitutions only. HGVS writes an
insertion or a deletion with `ins`, `del`, `dup`, or `delins`, and the VCF row
carries an extra anchor base that HGVS leaves out. Convert those rows with a
variant normalizer first, then check the result here.

## Check the shape offline

`pattern` mode checks that an id is well formed. It needs no network and
suits a first pass over a whole column.

```{r}
ids <- c(
  "19-44908822-C-T",
  "chr19-44908822-c-t",
  "19-44908822--T",
  "19:44908822:C:T"
)
res <- check_id(ids, source_db = "gnomad")
res[c("input", "valid", "suggestion")]
```

A lowercase allele is repairable, so the second id gets a suggestion. An empty
allele and the wrong separator have no repair. `repair_id()` applies every
suggestion in one call and returns the other values unchanged.

```{r}
repair_id(ids, source_db = "gnomad")
```

## Limits of a shape check

A well-formed id can still describe a variant that does not fit the genome.
All three ids below pass. The second states G as the reference base where the
genome has C, and the third points past the end of the chromosome.

```{r}
is_valid_id(
  c("19-44908822-C-T", "19-44908822-G-T", "19-999999999-C-T"),
  source_db = "gnomad"
)
```

The same holds for `spdi`, and for `hgvs` in `pattern` mode. A shape check
also cannot tell which genome build a gnomAD-style id counts on.

## Check a variant against the reference sequence

In `remote` mode, the `hgvs` source sends each well-formed description to the
Mutalyzer normalizer. Mutalyzer confirms that the reference sequence exists,
that the position lies inside it, and that the stated reference base is the
base found there. The lookup needs a network, so the code is shown with the
output of a run on 2026-11-15.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
candidates <- c(
  "NC_000019.10:g.44908822C>T", # the real variant
  "NC_000019.10:g.44908822G>T", # wrong reference base
  "NC_000019.10:g.999999999C>T" # past the end of the chromosome
)
res <- check_id(candidates, source_db = "hgvs", how = "remote")
res[c("input", "valid", "version")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   input                       valid version
#>   <chr>                       <lgl> <chr>
#> 1 NC_000019.10:g.44908822C>T  TRUE  2026-11-15T12:19:32Z
#> 2 NC_000019.10:g.44908822G>T  FALSE 2026-11-15T12:19:32Z
#> 3 NC_000019.10:g.999999999C>T FALSE 2026-11-15T12:19:33Z
```

The `version` column holds the time each answer was fetched. biobouncer stores
remote answers on disk and reuses them, so a repeated call returns the stored
answer with its first timestamp. Pass `refresh = TRUE` to ask the service
again.

The `gnomad` and `spdi` sources have `pattern` mode only. To check one of
those ids against the reference, write the same change as HGVS, as in the
build step above, and check that.

A variant that fits the reference is a possible variant. This check does not
say that anyone has observed it. The gnomAD lookup at the end of this article
does.

## Catch a coordinate from the wrong genome build

A gnomAD-style id does not say which build its position counts on. Writing
the variant as HGVS forces that choice, and the reference check then tests
it. `rs7412` sits at position 44908822 in GRCh38 and at 45412079 in GRCh37.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
is_valid_id(
  c(
    "NC_000019.10:g.44908822C>T", # GRCh38 position on the GRCh38 sequence
    "NC_000019.9:g.44908822C>T", # GRCh38 position on the GRCh37 sequence
    "NC_000019.9:g.45412079C>T" # GRCh37 position on the GRCh37 sequence
  ),
  source_db = "hgvs",
  how = "remote"
)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
```

The mismatched pair fails because GRCh37 has an A at position 44908822, where
the id states a C.

A single passing id proves little about the build. A coordinate from the
wrong build still passes when the other build happens to carry the same base
at that position. Check a sample of rows, since each id is a separate
request. On the wrong build, many of them fail.

## Check a record id against its database

An rsID or a ClinVar accession carries no information about the change, so
its shape says little. `remote` mode looks the id up in the database that
assigned it.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
res <- check_id(
  c("rs7412", "rs3200542", "rs999999999999"),
  source_db = "dbsnp",
  how = "remote"
)
res[c("input", "valid", "suggestion", "version")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   input          valid suggestion version
#>   <chr>          <lgl> <chr>      <chr>
#> 1 rs7412         TRUE  <NA>       2026-11-15T12:19:36Z
#> 2 rs3200542      FALSE rs7412     2026-11-15T12:19:36Z
#> 3 rs999999999999 FALSE <NA>       2026-11-15T12:19:36Z
```

dbSNP merged `rs3200542` into `rs7412`. The old id is reported as not valid,
and the current id is suggested. An rsID that dbSNP never issued gets no
suggestion.

For a ClinVar accession the lookup is an existence check only. A pass means
that ClinVar holds a record under that accession. A superseded accession is
not reported the way a merged rsID is.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
is_valid_id(
  c("VCV000017848", "VCV999999999"),
  source_db = "clinvar",
  how = "remote"
)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
```

A lookup raises an error when the service cannot be reached, or when it
answers with a rate limit or a server error. The result in those cases is
never `FALSE`.

## Check that gnomAD has observed a variant

biobouncer does not look a coordinate up in gnomAD. The
[bioclients](https://www.samuelbharti.com/bioclients/) package does.
`gnomad_variant_id()` builds the id that gnomAD takes, and
`gnomad_frequencies()` returns one row per id. Check the shape in between, so
an id with a wrong separator or an empty allele stops before the request.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(bioclients)

ids <- gnomad_variant_id(
  chrom = c("19", "chr19", "19"),
  pos = c(44908822, 44908684, 44908822),
  ref = c("C", "t", "G"),
  alt = c("T", "c", "T")
)
ids
#> [1] "19-44908822-C-T" "19-44908684-T-C" "19-44908822-G-T"

stopifnot(is_valid_id(ids, source_db = "gnomad"))

res <- gnomad_frequencies(ids)
freq <- biohttp::body_or_null(res)
if (is.null(freq)) {
  stop("gnomAD lookup: ", res$status, ". ", res$detail)
}
freq[c("variant_id", "rsid", "exome_af", "genome_af")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   variant_id      rsid     exome_af genome_af
#>   <chr>           <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 19-44908822-C-T rs7412     0.0738    0.0778
#> 2 19-44908684-T-C rs429358   0.148     0.157
#> 3 19-44908822-G-T <NA>      NA        NA
```

`gnomad_variant_id()` drops a `chr` prefix and writes the alleles in upper
case. `gnomad_frequencies()` returns no table when it refuses a request, for
example when the dataset is on another build, and the code stops on that. The
third id states the wrong reference base. gnomAD has no record of it, so its
row is `NA`.

A row of `NA` has more than one possible cause. gnomAD may have no record of
the variant. The request for that part of the batch may also have failed,
which the status does not show: a request that was sent has the status `ok`.
One id that gnomAD rejects fails every id sent with it. An id with an `N`
allele is such an id: it passes the shape check, and gnomAD rejects it.
`gnomad_frequency_by_id()` settles one id. Its status is `no_data` when gnomAD
has no record, and its `detail` field gives the reason.

An absent variant can still be a real one, because gnomAD holds only the
variants found in its samples. The reference check above tells a possible
variant from an impossible one.

The default dataset is `gnomad_r4`, which is on GRCh38. `gnomad_frequencies()`
and `gnomad_frequency_by_id()` take a `reference_genome` argument and refuse
a request when the dataset is on a different build. A refused request also
has the status `no_data`, and its `detail` field names the mismatch.
